clue.text: Exclusive people at club

blocks.note: Surface reading: the smart, select members of an exclusive nightclub
Setter's reading: people whose job is excluding others, the door staff who keep unwanted guests out

explanation.surface: A glimpse of the VIP crowd at a fashionable nightclub.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Exclusive' looks like an adjective meaning select; read it as 'doing the excluding' and it describes BOUNCERS, who turn people away at the door.
explanation.definitionFit: Door staff at a nightclub literally exclude unwanted guests, so they are the people doing the excluding.

clue.text: In suspense as a horse eats nothing

indicators.note: whatever eats something takes it inside

blocks.note: the article taken as it stands
gee-gee, a childish word for a horse
zero, the shape of the letter

explanation.surface: Onlookers hold their breath while a horse picks at its feed.
explanation.walkthrough: GG (gee-gee) is a nursery word for a horse and a crossword staple; the A sits in front and the O goes into the middle of it.
explanation.definitionFit: Being agog means eagerly waiting to learn what happens next, the same state as being held in suspense.

clue.text: Clock fitted with black wood

blocks.note: a device that measures time
standard abbreviation, as on pencils

explanation.surface: A clock case made from some dark wood, like ebony.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Black wood' reads as one phrase, ebony perhaps; split it, and 'black' is the B inserted while 'wood' alone is the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: Timber is cut wood used for building and carpentry, a straightforward synonym.

clue.text: One who is barely able to finish the act

definitions.text: One who is barely able to finish the act

blocks.clueFragment: barely able to finish the act
blocks.note: Surface reading: a struggling performer who only just manages to get through the show
Setter's reading: someone who finishes the act bare, wearing nothing

explanation.surface: A flagging performer who can hardly get to the end of the routine.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Barely' means 'only just' in the surface but 'naked' in the answer: the performer ends the act with no clothes on.
explanation.definitionFit: An exotic dancer takes off clothing during the routine and ends the performance nude.

clue.text: Bird takes gherkins, if desperate

indicators.note: desperate things are in a wild state, so the letters of the words before are thrown about

blocks.note: anagram fodder, ten letters

explanation.surface: A hungry bird will eat pickles if it gets desperate enough.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface makes 'takes' look like 'eats'; it only joins the definition to the fodder.
explanation.definitionFit: The kingfisher is a brightly coloured river bird that dives for fish, a specific example of a bird.

clue.text: Very protracted farewell

blocks.note: as in 'so good', meaning very good
drawn out in time

explanation.surface: A goodbye that drags on and on at the door.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface reads as one long farewell; split it, and 'Very' and 'protracted' each supply a word while 'farewell' defines.
explanation.definitionFit: 'So long' is an informal way of saying goodbye when parting from someone.

clue.text: Making do without love, fabricating about it

blocks.note: making something, or faking it
zero, as in a tennis score

explanation.surface: Someone lonely invents romances to cover for going without love.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Making do without love' reads as one phrase, but 'love' belongs to the wordplay as O, and 'about it' puts FORGING around that O.
explanation.definitionFit: To forgo something is to give it up or go without it, so forgoing means managing without.

clue.text: Wander about to escape tiny tormentor

blocks.note: to gad about is to roam idly from place to place
to flee, as in 'fly the country'

explanation.surface: Someone strolling around to get away from an annoying little pest.
explanation.walkthrough: 'About' looks like an indicator, but it is part of the phrase 'gad about'; GAD alone is the wandering.
explanation.definitionFit: A gadfly is a biting fly that pesters livestock, and figuratively a persistent irritating critic.

clue.text: Stand on three legs?

blocks.note: Surface reading: an instruction or feat, like a creature balancing on three limbs
Setter's reading: 'stand' as a noun, a support that has three legs

explanation.surface: A dog or a circus performer being asked to balance on three legs.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Stand' is a verb in the surface and a noun in the answer: the thing with three legs that a camera sits on.
explanation.definitionFit: A tripod is a three-legged support for cameras or telescopes, a kind of stand.

clue.text: Catch son and keep scolding

blocks.note: standard abbreviation in family trees
to nag is to scold persistently

explanation.surface: A parent who grabs their son and carries on telling him off.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Catch' looks like a verb about grabbing the boy; it is the noun, a hidden problem.
explanation.definitionFit: A catch is a hidden drawback, and a snag is exactly such an unexpected obstacle.

clue.text: Long in debt, splashing out for dog

indicators.note: splashing sends things flying in all directions, so the letters are scattered

blocks.note: anagram fodder, ten letters

explanation.surface: A spendthrift, deep in debt for ages, still splashes out on a pedigree pet.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Splashing out' is the spending in the surface; here it only signals that the letters are rearranged.
explanation.definitionFit: The Bedlington terrier is a lamb-like breed from Northumberland, in northern England, a specific type of dog.

clue.text: One raising boundary marker for sportsman

blocks.note: someone who puts up fences around a field
someone who duels with foil, épée or sabre

explanation.surface: A groundsman putting up a marker at the edge of a sports field.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface suggests cricket, where the boundary is the edge of the field; the sport is swordplay instead.
explanation.definitionFit: Both senses fit: a fence builder erects barriers, and an athlete in fencing competes with swords.

clue.text: It’s responsible for a holdup online

definitions.text: It’s responsible for a holdup online

blocks.note: Surface reading: a hacker or network fault causing an internet delay, or a web-based robbery
Setter's reading: something holding washing up on a line

explanation.surface: Blaming someone for a delay or a robbery on the internet.
explanation.walkthrough: Split 'online' into 'on line' and 'holdup' into 'hold up': the thing that holds washing up on the line.
explanation.definitionFit: A clip that fastens wet laundry to the washing line keeps it held up there.

clue.text: Returning mate slightly wounds birds

indicators.note: returning means going back the way it came

blocks.note: a friend
to wing is to hit only glancingly, as with a shot

explanation.surface: A partner comes home having injured some birds, perhaps on a shoot.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Wings' as a verb means to wound superficially, typically a bird clipped by a shot, which suits the surface nicely.
explanation.definitionFit: Lapwings are crested plovers of farmland and marsh, specific examples of birds.

clue.text: Dog that keeps sticking its nose in?

definitions.text: Dog that keeps sticking its nose in?

blocks.clueFragment: Dog that keeps sticking its nose in?
blocks.note: Surface reading: any sniffing dog pushing its nose into things
Setter's reading: prying into others' business, and also the name of a famous cartoon beagle

explanation.surface: An inquisitive hound poking its snout into everything.
explanation.walkthrough: The answer is both an adjective for a nosy person and the name of Charlie Brown's beagle in the Peanuts comic strip.
explanation.definitionFit: The Peanuts beagle is a famous cartoon hound, and being inquisitive or prying is being nosy.

clue.text: Two things found in the loo, one blown

blocks.clueFragment: Two things found in the loo
blocks.note: the toilet bowl, first of the two things

blocks.clueFragment: Two things found in the loo
blocks.note: the plumbing, second of the two things

explanation.surface: A plumber's inventory of a bathroom, with a blown pipe to fix.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Blown' suggests a burst pipe or fuse; it means played by blowing, as a wind instrument is.
explanation.definitionFit: Panpipes are a wind instrument of joined reeds, so they are played by blowing across them.

clue.text: Perhaps buttonhole old Catholic concealed

blocks.note: standard abbreviation
Roman Catholic
past tense of hide

explanation.surface: Perhaps an old Catholic hid away to avoid being cornered and harangued.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Buttonhole' tempts as the verb, to accost someone; it is the noun, a flower worn in a lapel, and 'Perhaps' marks the answer as one example.
explanation.definitionFit: An orchid is a flower sometimes worn pinned to a lapel at weddings, an example of such a corsage.

clue.text: Man of the people takes up central part in star comedy

indicators.note: the middle stretch of the following two words is what we keep, dropping their ends
in a down clue, taking something up lifts it so it reads from bottom to top

blocks.note: the middle eight letters, losing the first and last

explanation.surface: A populist figure lands the main role in a celebrity comedy.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Takes up central part' sounds like an actor taking a lead role; strip the S and Y from 'star comedy' and read the rest upwards.
explanation.definitionFit: A democrat believes in government by the people and champions ordinary citizens.

clue.text: A lot of snow, so unable to steer

blocks.note: taken as it stands
a heap of snow piled up by wind

explanation.surface: Heavy snowfall leaves a driver unable to control the car.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface pictures skidding on snow, but the answer is nautical: a boat floating without control.
explanation.definitionFit: A vessel that is adrift floats loose, carried by currents with no means of steering.

clue.text: Promoted over a woman, like Rees-Mogg

blocks.note: publicised heavily
slang for a woman, especially in Scotland

explanation.surface: Office politics: a man promoted ahead of a woman, just like one well-known politician.
explanation.walkthrough: Jacob Rees-Mogg is a British Conservative politician; the definition points not at his politics but at the joining mark in his surname.
explanation.definitionFit: Rees-Mogg is a double-barrelled surname joined by a short dash, which makes it hyphenated.

clue.text: Like a cowardy custard?

blocks.note: Surface reading: the British playground taunt for a coward
Setter's reading: both the coward and the dessert sauce share one colour

explanation.surface: Children mocking a timid friend in the playground.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Cowardy custard' is a British children's taunt for a scaredy-cat; custard is a sweet egg sauce whose colour also means cowardly.
explanation.definitionFit: Custard is a bright pastry-cream colour, and calling someone that colour is slang for cowardly.

clue.text: I’m quietly after small personnel; one this size?

blocks.note: abbreviation used on clothing labels
human resources, the personnel department
taken as it stands
piano, the musical direction for soft

explanation.surface: A quiet newcomer joining a small staff wonders if he is up to their size.
explanation.walkthrough: 'This size' refers back to 'small': a shrimp is a tiny creature, and slang for a very small person.
explanation.definitionFit: A shrimp is a little crustacean and a mocking nickname for a diminutive person, so it is something small.

clue.text: Notices a wicket in children’s recreation

blocks.note: spots
taken as it stands
cricket scorecard abbreviation

explanation.surface: Someone spots a wicket being taken during a children's game of cricket.
explanation.walkthrough: W for wicket comes from cricket scorecards; 'in' only joins the wordplay to the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: A seesaw is a playground plank that pivots in the middle, ridden by youngsters for fun.

clue.text: Sit in place as ordered, modelling material

indicators.note: the letters are put into a new order, as though by instruction

blocks.note: anagram fodder, ten letters

explanation.surface: An artist's model told to sit still in position for a sculptor.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Modelling' suggests a sitter posing, but it is shaping clay; Plasticine is a British brand of soft modelling clay.
explanation.definitionFit: Plasticine is a brand of soft coloured clay that children and animators shape into figures.

clue.text: The best? It’s groundbreaking

blocks.note: the choicest one, the one you would select first
a pickaxe literally breaks up earth

explanation.surface: A critic hailing something as the finest and innovative.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Groundbreaking' means innovative in the surface; taken literally, it describes a tool for breaking ground.
explanation.definitionFit: The pick of a group is its choicest member, and a pickaxe is the digging tool that splits hard earth.

clue.text: Football pitch, one in Richmond for example

blocks.note: football slang for the field of play
Richmond, in south-west London, has a huge royal deer enclosure

explanation.surface: A football ground in the London suburb of Richmond.
explanation.walkthrough: Richmond Park is a huge deer park in south-west London; British football commentators call the pitch 'the park'.
explanation.definitionFit: Commentators refer to the playing field as the park, and Richmond has a famous royal green space.

clue.text: Sailor’s prominent feature

blocks.note: the spinach-eating cartoon sailor
a bulging eye is a feature that sticks out

explanation.surface: The most noticeable trait of some seafarer.
explanation.walkthrough: Read the possessive 's' as 'is': the sailor is a prominent feature, a pop-eye, and the cartoon character is named after his bulging eye.
explanation.definitionFit: The cartoon seaman is famous for spinach, and a bulging eye sticks out on the face.

clue.text: Shake beaker, at this?

indicators.note: shaking mixes the contents, so the following letters are jumbled

blocks.note: anagram fodder, eight letters

explanation.surface: A lab worker stirring a mug or shaking a flask during a pause from work.
explanation.walkthrough: The whole clue is both the anagram and the definition: a pause when you might shake or stir a cup.
explanation.definitionFit: A short rest from work for a hot drink is when you might well swirl a mug.
